briefs.primary_keyword: writing english website copy as a non native speaker
secondary_keywords: should we hire a native english copywriter
briefs.working_title: Your English is fine. Your register is the problem
briefs.angle: Practical and unusually specific. Estonian companies write in English and the failures are not grammatical, which is why proofreading does not fix them. The real tells: formality calibrated too high because business English was learned from documents rather than conversation, abstract nouns where a verb belongs, feature lists in place of a claim, and translated idiom that lands oddly. Give the concrete repairs, including the read-aloud test, the one-sentence claim test, and the specific instruction to write the way you would explain it to a colleague rather than the way you would write a tender. Cover when to hire a native speaker and what to hire them for, which is editing and headline work rather than volume. Be careful to be useful rather than condescending; the premise is that the writing is competent and underperforming.
briefs.audience: Estonian founders and marketers writing their own English copy

briefs.primary_keyword: how to do competitor analysis for a small business
briefs.working_title: Most competitor analysis is a document nobody reads twice
briefs.angle: Opinion. The standard exercise produces a grid of features and a screenshot of somebody's homepage, gets presented once and never changes a decision. Argue that useful competitor work answers exactly one question: why does a buyer choose them over us, in their words rather than ours. Which means the sources are not their website but their reviews, their lost-deal behaviour and their job ads, since a job ad is the only place a company publishes what it is about to build. Cover what to stop collecting (feature grids, social follower counts, their blog cadence) and the three things worth tracking continuously. Keep clear of win-loss-analysis-for-small-business (23 Oct), which is about interviewing buyers, and of positioning-statement-examples (12 Oct).
briefs.audience: US founders and marketers doing this for the first time

briefs.primary_keyword: how to write a proposal that wins
secondary_keywords: what to include in a proposal
briefs.working_title: The proposal is not a document, it is a transcript
briefs.angle: Practical. Most proposals describe the seller: credentials, process, team, methodology. The ones that win read like a record of what the buyer said, in the buyer's words, with a price attached. Give the structure: their situation in their language first, the specific outcome, what is in and explicitly what is out, the price with one option rather than three tiers, and the next step with a date. Cover length honestly (shorter wins and here is why), what to do about the credentials section everybody insists on, and the single highest-value element, which is the sentence naming what you will not do. Reference how-to-run-a-discovery-call (25 Oct) as the input rather than repeating its questions, and do not rebuild should-i-put-pricing-on-my-website (15 Oct).
briefs.audience: US consultants, agencies and B2B sellers

briefs.primary_keyword: local sponsorship marketing for small business
briefs.working_title: The youth baseball banner, and what it is actually buying
briefs.angle: Practical and unsentimental. Local sponsorships get bought on obligation and sold on goodwill, and almost nobody states what they are for. Argue that there is exactly one mechanism that works, which is repeated exposure to a defined group of households who can already afford you, and that this makes the selection criteria measurable: how many of the right people see it, how often, for how long. Give the test for each common option (team kit, field banner, event booth, chamber membership, school programme) and the two that almost never pay. Cover the thing sponsors never negotiate for and should, which is the contact list or the speaking slot rather than the logo. Be fair about the genuine non-marketing reasons to do it.

briefs.primary_keyword: retainer vs project pricing for services
briefs.working_title: A retainer is a promise about your calendar, not your output
briefs.angle: Opinion from the seller's side, which is the gap: the published material is nearly all written for buyers. Argue that the retainer versus project choice is really a choice about who absorbs uncertainty, and that most firms pick the model that suits their cash flow and then discover it does not suit the work. Cover the failure mode of each honestly: retainers drift into unbounded support and die of resentment, projects end precisely when you have finally learned the client's business. Then the hybrid that actually holds, which is a defined project followed by a named smaller retainer with a stated scope of hours. Do not duplicate how-much-does-a-digital-marketing-agency-cost (27 Aug), which is the buyer's view, or how-to-price-services-in-india (24 Oct).

briefs.primary_keyword: festive season marketing for indian business
briefs.working_title: The festive fortnight is won in the week before it starts
briefs.angle: Practical and timely, since Diwali falls on 8 November this year. The useful content is not campaign ideas, it is the operational readiness that decides whether demand converts: stock and courier cutoffs, the customer service load, the pricing decision made in advance rather than in panic, and the post-festive slump nobody plans for. Cover what to stop doing in the week before (launching anything new), the specific things to pre-write, and the honest point that festive advertising costs rise enough that for some categories the right move is to sit out the peak and take the fortnight after. Verify the Diwali date before writing. Reference the demand window noted in local-seo-for-gyms-india (20 Oct) rather than repeating it.

briefs.working_title: What an IndiaMART lead actually is, before you buy a package
briefs.angle: Practical, and a real gap: nothing covers B2B marketplaces for Indian manufacturers. Be concrete about the mechanism, which is that a buy-side enquiry is distributed to several sellers at once, so the channel rewards response speed over everything else and the economics only work if somebody answers within minutes. Cover what to fix on the listing, the specification detail that filters time-wasters, and the honest arithmetic of a paid package against the enquiry volume it produces. Then the strategic point: a marketplace enquiry is a price comparison by default, so the work is moving the conversation off the platform to something that is not a bidding war. Keep clear of seo-for-exporters-india (5 Oct) and do not restate the Justdial argument from how-to-get-more-reviews-indian-business (26 Oct).

briefs.primary_keyword: cash on delivery returns d2c india
briefs.working_title: COD is not a payment method, it is a free option you wrote for the customer
briefs.angle: Opinion with real economics. Cash on delivery is treated as a conversion aid and it is actually an option contract the seller hands over for nothing: the customer decides at the door whether to complete the purchase, and the seller pays shipping both ways when they decline. Argue that the honest way to see return-to-origin is as the price of that option, and that most Indian D2C brands report revenue before knowing it. Cover the levers that genuinely work (partial advance, prepaid incentive, address and pin-code confirmation, holding first-time buyers to prepaid in high-RTO pin codes) and the one that does not, which is simply removing COD in a market where it still drives a large share of orders. Be careful with RTO figures and attribute or decline them.

briefs.primary_keyword: what percentage of revenue should go to marketing
secondary_keywords: how much should a small business spend on marketing
briefs.working_title: The percentage-of-revenue budget is a rule for companies that already won
briefs.angle: Opinion, but the debunk is already done and must NOT be repeated: annual-marketing-plan-small-business (19 Oct) covers why percentage-of-revenue is survivor arithmetic, with the Gartner and Duke numbers. Link to it in one line and move on. Spend this whole article on the arithmetic that replaces it, which that post did not have room for. Build the budget from the bottom: what it currently costs to acquire one customer through the one channel that demonstrably works, how many customers the business needs to add, and what capacity exists to serve them. Cover the two failure modes of that method, which are that most owners do not know their real acquisition cost and that the number it produces is often larger than the business can fund, and say what to do in each case rather than retreating to a percentage. Then the one case where percentage-of-revenue is genuinely correct: a mature business with stable demand budgeting to hold position, where it is a maintenance control rather than a growth decision. US market, dollars.

retired.primary_keyword: how long does seo take
secondary_keywords: when will i see seo results
retired.working_title: How long does SEO take, and when should you stop waiting?
retired.angle: Opinion, against the consensus. The whole first page of results for this query says three to six months and almost none of it cites anything. Ahrefs' own data (updated May 2025, Patrick Stox) says the opposite shape: only 1.74% of newly published pages reach the top 10 within a year, 6.11% on their fairer filter, and 40.82% of the pages that did rank got there inside the first month. So the outcome is closer to bimodal than gradual, which makes three to six months the period in which, on that data, the least new information arrives. Resolve the apparent contradiction with the age data (72.9% of top 10 pages are over three years old, average number one is five years old): incumbency is accumulated history on an updated URL, not a new page slowly ripening. Give decision checkpoints rather than outcome promises, and never a timeline to page one. State the caveats plainly: vendor crawler data, the 40.82% is conditional on pages that ranked, and top-10 placement no longer means traffic.

So judge it on whether the guest list is your pipeline, not on downloads. Be specific about the cases where it genuinely fails: a category with no interesting practitioners, a host who does not enjoy it, and the content treadmill that kills most shows by episode eleven. retired.angle: Opinion. For a company in a 1.3 million person market, the channel looks like the obvious answer to international expansion, and it usually fails for a reason worth stating: a reseller sells what is already easy to sell. Handing an unproven product to a partner outsources the hardest unsolved problem, which is working out why anybody buys, to the party least motivated to solve it. Argue the sequence: you have to win the first several customers in a market directly, painfully, in order to know what to hand over. Then cover what a partner actually needs to succeed, what exclusivity costs you, and the single question that predicts whether a channel deal works, which is whether the partner has ever sold something in this category before or merely has the relationships. retired.working_title: Your best channel did not break. It matured
retired.angle: Analysis. When a channel that carried a business for years softens, the instinct is to fix it, and the fix usually works for one quarter and then stops. Argue that there are three different diagnoses with the same symptom: the platform changed the rules, the channel got competitive enough that your cost caught up with everybody else's, or your own offer stopped being differentiated and the channel is simply reporting that honestly. Only the first is a marketing problem. Give the test that separates them, which is whether your competitors' cost rose too. The uncomfortable conclusion is that a saturated channel is a pricing and positioning signal arriving through a dashboard. Do not re-run do-we-need-a-rebrand (14 Oct) or the avoidance frame.
